n: In this lecture we study pyridine and piperidine derivatives. The outline: their toxicological significance, isolation from physical evidence and methods of analysis. Key terms: microcrystalloscopic analysis; nicotine, anabasine, pachycarpine, arecoline, coniine. The next part of the outline, that is, tropane and quinoline derivatives: atropine, hyoscyamine, scopolamine, quinine, will be covered in a separate lecture.

t: Characteristics of the group: liquid alkaloids
n: Characteristics of the group. The aim of this lecture is to introduce the liquid alkaloids, that is, pyridine, piperidine and quinolizidine derivatives, and their analysis. Anabasine and nicotine belong to the pyridine derivatives, and pachycarpine to the quinolizidine derivatives. Sections: nicotine, anabasine, pachycarpine, coniine and arecoline. Nicotine occurs in tobacco, anabasine in Anabasis aphylla and partly in tobacco, pachycarpine in Sophora and in the leaves of Thermopsis, and coniine in spotted hemlock.

Sources and uses of the liquid alkaloids. Nicotine occurs in tobacco, anabasine in Anabasis aphylla and tobacco, pachycarpine in Sophora and Thermopsis, and coniine in spotted hemlock. Arecoline occurs in the fruit of the areca palm, in an amount of 0.1-0.5 %; its bromide salt is used in medicine and veterinary practice. Remember: all liquid alkaloids are isolated by steam distillation and extracted in an alkaline medium.

Nicotine: source and accompanying alkaloids. The tobacco plant contains the alkaloid nicotine in an amount from 0.6 % to 8 %; the chemical name is pyridine-3-N-methylpyrrolidine. The most important accompanying substances: nornicotine, nicotyrine, methylanabasine and anabasine. Nicotine in pure form was isolated in 1828 and synthesised in 1935.

Physical properties of nicotine. As the base, nicotine is a colourless, odourless oily liquid. Boiling point 246.1 °C. The refractive index at 20 °C is 1.5280. Nicotine is optically active: the base rotates polarised light to the left, and its salts to the right.

Solubility and stability of nicotine. In water below 60 °C it is very soluble and miscible with water in all proportions; at 60-210 °C it is poorly soluble. It is freely soluble in organic solvents. The aqueous solution is alkaline, and it forms crystalline salts with acids. Like other liquid alkaloids it is volatile; in air it is rapidly oxidised to nicotyrine and gradually darkens. Poorly purified nicotine smells of tobacco.

When is testing for nicotine carried out? Testing for nicotine is carried out when there is a special instruction from the investigating authorities. It is also carried out if, during the chemical examination, the chloroform residue is oily and has a characteristic smell. The pathological-anatomical examination of the corpse gives no characteristic signs with respect to nicotine.

Use of nicotine and its toxicological significance. Because nicotine is widely used in the national economy, its toxicological significance is high. It is used as a contact insecticide and insectofungicide. Nicodust is a mixture of 5 g of nicotine sulphate and 95 g of lime; tobacco dust and tobacco infusions are also used against pests. Preparations containing nicotine are not used in medical practice; in veterinary practice they are used to treat scabies. In the pharmaceutical industry it is the raw material for the synthesis of nicotinic acid by oxidation.

t: Sources of poisoning: naswar and smoking
n: Sources of poisoning. Places where poisoning is possible: tobacco products, cigarette factories, tobacco plantations and leaf-drying sites. Because naswar is widespread in Central Asia, unpleasant incidents with nicotine occur. In addition to tobacco, naswar contains slaked lime, chewing gum and oily substances that enhance its effect. When smoking a chillum and other smoking devices, nicotine is constantly absorbed through the airways and lungs.

Pharmacological action of nicotine. Nicotine has a poisonous effect on nerve cells: it first slightly stimulates nervous activity, and then leads to paralysis. The dose of nicotine that can lead to a person's death is 0.01-0.08 g. It poisons the endings of the central and autonomic nerves and disrupts the function of the ganglia. Pharmacokinetics according to the qualification data: pKa 3.2 and 7.9, at 25 °C; T½ 28-84 minutes; Vd 1.0 L/kg.

Signs of poisoning. For a person who has never smoked, 1-2 cigarettes, that is, 1-4 mg of nicotine, cause a severe headache, dizziness and weakness. Diarrhoea, vomiting, rapid heartbeat and difficulty in breathing are observed. Salivation, shortness of breath and peculiar convulsive phenomena may also occur. In tobacco and cigarette factories the concentration of tobacco dust in the air must not exceed 0.003 mg/l.

Absorption and elimination of nicotine. Nicotine is rapidly absorbed by the mucous membrane of the mouth and in the lungs, and is also rapidly absorbed through healthy skin. In smoking, up to 90-98 % of the nicotine enters the body with the smoke and is absorbed into the blood through the lungs. In women who smoke, it passes through the blood into breast milk and poisons the nursing infant. It is eliminated from the body through the airways, and partly in the urine and sweat.

Metabolism of nicotine. Nicotine is oxidised and demethylated in liver tissue; the metabolites are excreted in the urine. Over 24 hours, 5 % is excreted in the urine unchanged and as metabolites. Shares of the metabolites: cotinine 10 %, hydroxycotinine 35 %, nicotine-1’-N-oxide 4 %, norcotinine 5 %.

Isolating nicotine from physical evidence. Besides the methods with acidified alcohol or water, the steam distillation method is also recommended. It is extracted with organic solvents partly in an acidic and mainly in an alkaline medium. That is, it is isolated from physical evidence with acidified water or alcohol, in an alkaline medium.

t: Nicotine: precipitation, Dragendorff and Reinecke's salt
n: Nicotine: precipitation, Dragendorff's reagent and Reinecke's salt. Nicotine forms a precipitate with the general precipitating reagents of alkaloids. If hydrochloric acid and Dragendorff's reagent are added dropwise to the residue, reddish crystals in the shape of “X” and “K”, resembling flying birds, are formed. The detection limit is 1 µg; anabasine and coniine also give crystals, but of a different shape. With Reinecke's salt, a freshly prepared solution, and HCl, prismatic red-pink crystals are formed; the detection limit is 1.2 µg.

Colour reactions of nicotine. Under the action of formaldehyde and concentrated nitric acid, a red compound is formed; anabasine does not give this reaction. Under the action of n-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde and concentrated HCl it gives a pink compound that turns violet. In the presence of potassium cyanide and chloramine B, glutaconic aldehyde is formed; if barbituric acid is added to it, a yellow-reddish colour appears.

t: Nicotine: TLC, UV spectrum, biological test
n: Nicotine: TLC, UV spectrum and biological test. In TLC the mobile phase is hexane-acetone, 4:1; when sprayed with acidified iodoplatinate reagent, Rf=0.4, and a blue spot is formed. In the UV spectrum a solution in 0.1 N H2SO4 has an absorption maximum at a wavelength of 260 nm. In the pharmacological test, if a nicotine solution is dropped on the hind part of a frog's body, after a few minutes the frog freezes in a convulsive posture as if sitting. The amount is determined by the photoelectrocolorimetric and SP methods.

Anabasine: source and uses. Anabasine is an alkaloid found in the plant Anabasis aphylla and partly in tobacco; a colourless oily substance, freely soluble in organic solvents. Anabasine hydrochloride in tablets is used against smoking. In agriculture, as anabadust, it is used against insects, and in animal husbandry against lice, ringworm and scabies of animals. Composition of anabadust: 7 % anabasine sulphate and 93 % slaked lime.

Anabasine: poisoning and isolation. Its action is similar to nicotine: it is absorbed through the airways and skin, stimulates nervous activity, and then paralyses the autonomic nerve fibres; blood pressure rises. Symptoms: salivation, vomiting, diarrhoea, yellowing of the body and hair loss. It is excreted in the urine; its metabolites are little studied. For isolation, water acidified with sulphuric acid and steam distillation are used; extraction with an organic solvent is carried out mainly in an alkaline medium.

Anabasine: precipitation and crystal reactions. With Dragendorff's reagent, small red-brown pointed crystals are formed; coniine and nicotine give crystals of a different shape. With picric acid it gives a yellow precipitate, whereas nicotine does not. With Bouchardat's reagent, a red-brown precipitate; with the cobalt thiocyanate complex, a cluster of pink crystals; with Reinecke's salt, needle-like crystals are formed.

Colour reactions of anabasine. With perhydrol and concentrated H2SO4 it gives a red colour. With a vanillin crystal and 1-2 drops of concentrated H2SO4 it gives a red or cherry-red colour. With KCN, chloramine B and barbituric acid it forms a yellow-brown colour.

Distinguishing nicotine and anabasine. With Dragendorff's reagent, nicotine gives crystals in the shape of “X” and “K”, and anabasine gives pointed crystals. With picric acid, anabasine gives a yellow precipitate; nicotine does not. With formaldehyde and concentrated HNO3, nicotine gives a red compound; anabasine does not. With Reinecke's salt, nicotine forms prismatic crystals, and anabasine needle-like crystals.

Quantitative analysis of anabasine. The amount is determined by the SP method. The photoelectrocolorimetric method is based on the formation of glutaconic aldehyde by anabasine with KCN and chloramine. Glutaconic aldehyde forms a yellow-brown colour with barbituric acid, and it is this colour that is measured by photoelectrocolorimetry.

Pachycarpine: source and uses. Pachycarpine is contained in the aerial parts of Sophora and in the leaves of Thermopsis. As the base it is a clear, colourless oily liquid; it changes on standing in air. In medicine it is used as the iodide, which is freely soluble in water and alcohol. Uses: spasm of peripheral vessels, hypertension, and, in gynaecology, to increase uterine contractions.

Pachycarpine: poisoning and isolation. Pachycarpine does not accumulate in the body and leaves the body within a day. When taken above the therapeutic dose, for example for abortion, nausea, vomiting, dizziness and difficulty in breathing are observed; the pupil dilates, and cyanosis and convulsions appear. Besides the acidified alcohol and water method, it is also isolated by electrodialysis. The main part is extracted under alkaline conditions.

t: Pachycarpine: reaction for the iodide anion
n: The reaction for the iodide anion in pachycarpine. After extraction with chloroform, the ammoniacal aqueous solution is acidified with 10 % H2SO4, against litmus. Then it is shaken with 2-3 drops of 1 % NaNO2 and 3 ml of chloroform. As a result I2 dissolves in the chloroform layer, and the layer is stained violet.

Pachycarpine: crystal and other reactions. With Bouchardat's reagent, yellow crystals in the shape of an oak leaf are formed; with the cobalt thiocyanate complex, light-blue prismatic crystals. With picric acid, a yellow-green crystalline precipitate; with the copper iodide complex, it gives a cluster of yellow crystals. In bromine oxidation, if filter paper impregnated with the solution is held in bromine vapour, a yellow colour appears, which turns red on heating with ammonia. In quantitative analysis, the bromophenol blue complex is extracted with chloroform and determined by the extraction-photometric method.

Coniine: source and properties. Coniine, that is, propylpiperidine, was isolated by Hofmann from spotted hemlock; Ladenburg developed its synthesis in 1886. The body of spotted hemlock contains about 2 % alkaloids, half of which is coniine. It is a colourless oily liquid resembling the smell of mouse urine; in air it is rapidly oxidised and turns brown. It is freely soluble in water, especially cold water, 1:100; on heating it becomes cloudy. The aqueous solution is strongly alkaline; it distils readily with steam.

Sources of coniine poisoning. Poisoning most often results from the use of spotted hemlock in place of dill or parsley, or its root in place of horseradish. This kind of poisoning is more common among animals and children; grazing livestock where this plant grows is dangerous. Poisoning also occurs when hemlock seeds get mixed with aniseed. In ancient Greece, hemlock extract was mixed with opium and given to the condemned; Socrates was executed in this way.

Action and clinical picture of coniine. Coniine and the accompanying alkaloids paralyse the autonomic nerves and the central nervous system; conhydrine is a poison 18 times stronger than coniine. Because of its good solubility in water, coniine is rapidly absorbed; symptoms appear after a few minutes: paralysis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, profuse sweating. Consciousness is preserved, and vision weakens. First breathing is strengthened, then the respiratory nerve is paralysed and breathing stops, while the heart beats for some time; death usually occurs after 1-2 hours.

Features of the examination for coniine. Pathomorphological examination gives no characteristic signs of coniine; physical evidence is examined by the methods of toxicological chemistry, and plant parts by pharmacognostic analysis. Alkaloids are excreted through the respiratory and urinary tracts, so besides pieces of stomach and intestine, the urinary bladder and blood are also sent. According to the methods of A.V. Akhutina, coniine in a biological object remains unchanged for a long time; it has been detected even after 4 months. The smallest quantity lethal for a person is 0.5-1.0 g.

Isolating coniine. The object is distilled with steam, with soda and water, or with acidified alcohol. From the isolate, coniine is extracted with ether in an alkaline medium. After the ether has evaporated, the smell and physical state of the residue are determined. The residue is usually an oily yellowish liquid.

Coniine: crystal and colour reactions. With Dragendorff's reagent, red microcrystals in the shape of rhombi are formed, with a sensitivity of 3.5 µg. With HCl vapour, coniine gives coniine chloride, that is, twisted needle-like microcrystals, with a sensitivity of 0.33 µg. With ammoniacal CuSO4, CS2 and benzene, the benzene layer is stained brown-yellow, with a sensitivity of 1 µg.

Coniine: TLC and spectra. In TLC the mobile phase is methanol and concentrated ammonium hydroxide, 100:1.5; with acidified iodoplatinate Rf=0.26. In the UV spectrum a solution in 0.2 N sulphuric acid has an absorption maximum at 266 nm, and a solution in 0.1 N alkali at 262 and 268 nm. In the IR spectrum, bands at 1033, 1007, 1575, 1300, 1139 and 1078 cm⁻¹ are given. The amount is determined spectrophotometrically from the UV spectrum.

Arecoline: source and properties. Arecoline is the methyl ester of N-methyltetrahydronicotinic acid; the fruit of the areca palm contains up to 0.1-0.5 per cent. The alkaloid was identified in 1866, and a method of synthesis was found in 1907. It is a colourless, thick, oily liquid, boiling point 209 °C; it distils readily with steam. In medicine and veterinary practice the salt of arecoline with hydrobromic acid is used, because it is more stable in air.

Toxicological significance and metabolism of arecoline. It is a strongly poisonous substance: taking more than 0.5-1.5 mg causes symptoms of poisoning. The pupil constricts sharply, the activity of the pancreas increases, and the intestines contract strongly; blood pressure falls and salivation occurs. Under the action of acid and alkali it is hydrolysed, forming methyl alcohol and arecaidine; arecaidine is N-methyltetrahydronicotinic acid. It persists for a long time in the organs of a corpse: 2 mg of arecoline in 100 g of biological object was detected even after 2-2.5 months.

Isolation and detection of arecoline. Sodium bicarbonate is recommended for the alkaline medium. Arecoline is extracted in an alkaline medium after extraction with acidic alcohol or water and steam distillation. With Dragendorff's reagent, on standing for 30 minutes in the presence of 0.1 N HCl, red microcrystals in the shape of “x” are formed; the detection limit is 0.2 µg. With picric acid, dark green spherulites form, then prismatic crystals; the detection limit is also 0.2 µg. In TLC, methanol and concentrated ammonium hydroxide 100:1.5, with potassium permanganate Rf=0.53, a white spot on a pinkish background.

Let us compare the crystals with Dragendorff's reagent. Nicotine gives crystals in the shape of “X” and “K”, detection limit 1 µg; anabasine gives pointed crystals. Coniine gives red rhomb-shaped microcrystals, 3.5 µg. Arecoline gives red “x”-shaped microcrystals, 0.2 µg. Thus the crystal shape helps to distinguish the substances from one another.

The general scheme of analysis. The first stage is isolation: acidified alcohol, or water, or steam distillation, followed by alkaline extraction. The second stage is confirmation: precipitating reagents, microcrystalline and colour reactions, and TLC. Then UV and IR spectra are recorded. The amount is determined by SP, photoelectrocolorimetry or extraction photometry.

Conclusion on the topic. Nicotine, anabasine, pachycarpine, coniine and arecoline are liquid, volatile alkaloids, and isolation by steam distillation is their common method. The pathological-anatomical picture gives no characteristic signs for nicotine, coniine and arecoline, so chemical-toxicological analysis is decisive. For identification, precipitating reagents, microcrystalline and colour reactions, TLC, and UV and IR spectra are used; the amount is determined by the SP and photoelectrocolorimetric methods.
